title: You thought you were fine.
paragraphs: You thought you were fine.
Not perfect—but fine.
You said the prayers. You showed up when it mattered. You called yourself a Christian, and nobody really questioned it. From the outside, your life had just enough “God” in it to feel safe.
But then Jesus says something that should shake you all the way to your core:
“Then I will declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness.’” (Matthew 7:23)
Read that again.

Not “I knew you once.”
Not “you knew about Me.”
Not even “you tried.”
“I never knew you.”
That means it’s possible to live an entire life thinking you belong to Him… and be completely unknown by Him.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
The scene Jesus describes isn’t casual. It’s not symbolic. It’s judgment. Final. Irreversible.
People are standing before Him—confident, even bold. They’re not atheists. They’re not denying Him. Listen to what they say just one verse earlier:
“Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in Your name, cast out demons in Your name, and do many mighty works in Your name?” (Matthew 7:22)

They used His name.
They did spiritual things.
They had visible power.
And still… rejected.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Jesus doesn’t deny their works.
He denies the relationship.
“I never knew you.”

That word “knew” isn’t casual awareness. It’s deep, personal, relational. The kind of knowing that transforms you. The kind of knowing that changes what you love, what you hate, how you live when no one is watching.

You can know Scripture and not know Him.
You can serve in ministry and not know Him.
You can look clean in public and still be practicing sin in private.
God saw it.
You knew.
And that’s where it turns.
Because Jesus exposes the root issue in one phrase:
“you who practice lawlessness.”

Not “you who made mistakes.”
Not “you who struggled.”
Practice.
A pattern. A lifestyle. Ongoing rebellion dressed up in religious activity.
This is the person who says “Lord” with their mouth… but refuses Him with their life.

Titus 1:16 says it plainly:
“They profess to know God, but they deny Him by their works.”
That’s the tension.
Confession without transformation is not salvation.
And this is where many get it wrong—dangerously wrong.

They think Christianity is about doing enough good to outweigh the bad.
They think proximity to church equals closeness to Christ.
They think using His name means belonging to Him.
But salvation was never about your performance.

Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace you have been saved through faith… not a result of works, so that no one may boast.”
So what went wrong in Matthew 7?
It wasn’t that they didn’t do enough.
It’s that they never repented.
They never surrendered.
They never trusted in Jesus as Savior and Lord—they just used Him.

There was no brokenness over sin.
No turning away.
No new heart.
Just religion.
And religion without Christ will walk you straight into judgment thinking you’re safe.
This is the part people avoid.
Because it forces you to ask something uncomfortable:
Do I actually know Him… or do I just know about Him?
Because when you truly know Jesus, something shifts.

2 Corinthians 5:17 says:
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.”
Not perfection—but transformation.

Sin no longer feels normal.
Conviction becomes real.
Grace becomes everything.
You don’t just say “Lord”—you follow Him.
And yes, you’ll still stumble. You’ll still fight. But your life won’t be defined by practicing lawlessness—it will be marked by repentance.
That’s the difference.

One life hides behind religious activity.
The other is broken before God and made new by grace.

Two people can stand in the same church…
Sing the same songs…
Say the same words…
And one will hear, “Well done.”
The other…
“I never knew you.”
That’s not fear tactics.
That’s truth.
And it’s mercy that you’re hearing it now—not then.
Because right now, the door is still open.
Right now, repentance is still available.
Right now, you can stop pretending.
You can stop performing.
You can come to Jesus—not with your works, not with your résumé—but with your sin, your need, your surrender.

1 John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us… and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That’s the Gospel.

You are more sinful than you admit…
But more loved than you realize…
Because Jesus took the judgment you deserve.
On the cross, He was rejected…
So you could be accepted.
But only if you come to Him on His terms.

Not halfway.
Not pretending.
Fully.
So be honest.
If you stood before Him today—would He say He knows you?
Or would that verse expose everything you’ve been hiding behind?
Say it plainly—“Jesus, I don’t want to be unknown to You.” Let that be real, not just words.
There’s more depth waiting for you—real understanding, real correction, real growth. Not surface-level faith, but the kind that actually transforms you from the inside out.
Follow this path if you’re done playing games with God.
